content: 1. Hand hygiene stations and designated areas for donning and doffing personal protective equipment (PPE), as well as spaces for decontamination, must be established to ensure safe practices. 2. Cleaning staff who have previously worked in Ebola care facilities and have been trained in safe cleaning procedures should be identified and provided with a comprehensive briefing before commencing their duties. 3. The health and safety of staff must be closely monitored, and any injuries or illnesses should be promptly reported. 4. An occupational health and safety officer should ideally collaborate with the infection prevention and control (IPC) officer to conduct the initial assessment and oversee the monitoring of the decommissioning process. 5. Facilities should not be reopened or repurposed until the decommissioning process is safely completed, documented using a checklist, and formally signed off by the IPC officer(s) following a final inspection. 6. To address potential social and psychological concerns about repurposing former Ebola care facilities (e.g., schools or community centers), district authorities and social mobilization officers should develop effective communication strategies to reassure healthcare workers and the public about the safety of these facilities after decontamination. 7. Where feasible, visual improvements such as repainting walls, landscaping, or refreshing furniture should be considered to enhance the acceptability and appeal of the facility for its new purpose. 8. In high-risk zones (red zones) where suspected or confirmed Ebola patients were treated, cleaners must wear full PPE as per WHO recommendations. This includes double gloves, a disposable gown or coverall resistant to blood and body fluids, a waterproof apron, eye protection (goggles or face shield), a mask, and rubber boots. 9. In low-risk zones (green zones), such as areas where PPE is donned or office spaces around treatment units, lower-level PPE (disposable gown, heavy-duty gloves, mask, face shield, and boots) may be used. 10. If there is no clear distinction between red and green zones, cleaners should wear full PPE at all times during cleaning procedures. 11. Standard procedures for donning and doffing PPE must be meticulously followed, as they would be during the operational phase of an Ebola facility. 12. All non-intact objects or equipment, such as damaged furniture or mattresses, should be safely removed, disposed of, and incinerated. 13. Intact surfaces that can withstand rigorous cleaning should be cleaned and disinfected thoroughly. Items to be decontaminated should be carefully recorded, labeled, and documented. 14. Solid waste generated during cleaning, including dirty cloths, towels, and PPE, should be placed in leak-proof plastic bags, collected in covered bins designated as infectious waste, and incinerated. 15. Sharp objects and clinical equipment should be placed in puncture-resistant waste containers and incinerated. 16. Cleaning should always proceed from clean areas to dirty areas to prevent cross-contamination. The area where PPE is removed should be the last to be cleaned. 17. Dry sweeping with a broom or cleaning with dry rags should never be done, as this can spread virus particles. Instead, use moistened cloths to minimize airborne contamination. 18. Disinfectants should be freshly prepared daily if made locally, and cleaning/disinfectant solutions should be changed every 2-3 hours during use to prevent contamination. 19. Spills of biological waste, such as blood or bodily fluids, should be cleaned immediately. The soiled area should be covered with a rag or paper towel to prevent splashes, and the spill should be wiped up and disposed of in designated infectious waste containers. 20. Environmental surfaces, including furniture, walls, and doors, should be cleaned and disinfected using a solution containing 5000 ppm available free chlorine or another suitable disinfectant. Surfaces should be allowed to dry naturally. 21. If surfaces are rinsed with water during cleaning, they should be dried with rags before applying disinfectant to avoid diluting the recommended concentration. 22. Reusable materials should be decontaminated through thorough cleaning and disinfection, while non-reusable items should be safely disposed of. 23. Wastewater treatment and disposal must be carefully managed to prevent the spread of fecal-oral pathogens, such as cholera or poliovirus, which could trigger concurrent outbreaks. 24. Temporary latrines should be disinfected, dismantled, and disposed of through incineration, burning, or deep burial. The pit should be backfilled with packed soil or debris and demarcated with signage and GPS coordinates. 25. Permanent latrines intended for reuse should be cleaned and disinfected. If the pit is more than two-thirds full, desludging should be performed according to national guidelines. Once decontaminated, the latrine can be safely used again. 26. Septic or holding tanks should be sealed and backfilled with soil or debris if they are not to be reused. If they are to be reused, they should only be emptied if more than two-thirds full, and desludging should follow national guidelines. 27. Temporary showers should be treated similarly to latrines, with the superstructure disinfected and disposed of, and the shower pit backfilled to ground level. 28. Water infrastructure, such as pipes, can be reused after disinfection with a 0.5% chlorine solution. Sanitary surveys and microbiological testing should be conducted for water points, and shock chlorination (1%) may be used for shallow or hand-dug wells. 29. Communities should be informed that decontamination has been completed to provide reassurance about the safety of the facilities.
